items.prompt: Why do many leaves turn yellow and orange in autumn instead of simply staying green until they fall?

options.label: The tree manufactures new yellow and orange pigments especially for autumn
options.feedback: These pigments aren't newly made in autumn at all; they were already present in the leaf, just outnumbered and covered up by the dominant green pigment all summer.

options.label: As the dominant green pigment breaks down, yellow and orange pigments that were there all along become visible
options.feedback: Those colours were sitting in the leaf the whole summer, simply overwhelmed by far more green pigment until that green pigment starts to break down.

options.label: Cold temperatures physically bleach the green colour out of the leaf
options.feedback: Cold on its own doesn't strip pigment from a leaf; the actual change happening is the tree deliberately breaking its green pigment down and reclaiming the material.

options.label: Falling sunlight levels stop the leaf from reflecting any colour at all
options.feedback: A leaf reflecting less light overall would look darker rather than switching to a completely different colour, so a drop in total sunlight doesn't explain the specific shift toward yellow and orange.

items.ok_line: Those colours were there the whole summer, just hidden under more green.
items.ko_title: Not new pigment, not bleaching, not less light
items.ko_line: The pigments responsible for the autumn colour aren't being made fresh — think about what happens once the dominant summer colour is removed.
items.exp_title: The colours were there all along
items.exp_text: A green leaf actually contains several pigments at once, but during the growing season the green pigment is present in such large amounts that it drowns out every other colour. As autumn approaches, the tree deliberately breaks that green pigment down, and once it's gone the yellow and orange pigments that were quietly present the whole time are finally visible. The leaf hasn't gained a new colour; it has simply lost the one that was hiding the others.

items.prompt: Why does a tree actively break down the green pigment in its leaves each autumn rather than just leaving it in place until the leaf drops?

options.label: The pigment would poison the tree if it stayed in a dying leaf
options.feedback: Green pigment isn't toxic to the tree; leaving it in place wouldn't harm the tree, which is why breaking it down is about salvage rather than about avoiding danger.

options.label: The pigment molecule contains valuable nitrogen, and breaking it down lets the tree reclaim that nitrogen before the leaf falls
options.feedback: Rather than let a nitrogen-rich molecule fall to the ground still locked inside the pigment, the tree dismantles it and pulls that nitrogen back into its twigs before the leaf drops.

options.label: Breaking the pigment down makes the leaf lighter so it detaches more easily
options.feedback: The mass of pigment in a leaf is far too small to meaningfully affect how easily it detaches; the leaf separates through an entirely different mechanism at its base.

options.label: Sunlight in autumn destroys the pigment on its own, without any effort from the tree
options.feedback: This breakdown is an active, controlled process carried out by the leaf's own cells, not a passive effect of weaker autumn sunlight simply degrading the pigment.

items.ok_line: That green pigment is rich in nitrogen the tree doesn't want to waste.
items.ko_title: Not poison, not weight, not sunlight alone
items.ko_line: Think about what valuable material is locked up inside that pigment molecule, and why a tree wouldn't want to lose it.
items.exp_text: The green pigment in a leaf is built around a good deal of nitrogen, an element a tree can never simply pull out of the air the way it pulls carbon, and has to gather slowly and expensively through its roots instead. Rather than let that nitrogen drop to the ground still locked inside the pigment along with the rest of the falling leaf, the tree's own enzymes take the pigment apart and ship the freed nitrogen back into the twigs for storage. What looks like simple decay is really a planned salvage operation, reclaiming a costly material before the leaf that held it is let go.

items.prompt: Some tree leaves turn vivid red or purple in autumn while others of the same species stay yellow. What produces that red or purple colour?

options.label: A different pigment that the leaf actively produces fresh in autumn, rather than one that was already present and simply unmasked
options.feedback: Unlike the yellows and oranges that were hidden in the leaf all summer, this red pigment is newly manufactured by the leaf specifically during autumn, likely offering the leaf some protection while it finishes reclaiming its nutrients.

options.label: The same pigment responsible for yellow, just concentrated at a higher level
options.feedback: Concentrating the yellow-and-orange pigment further would only intensify that same colour, not shift it into an entirely different colour like red or purple.

options.label: A build-up of the leaf's own dying, decayed cell material
options.feedback: Decaying cell material tends to turn brown rather than a vivid red or purple; this colour comes from an actual pigment being produced, not simply from cells breaking down.

options.label: Frost damage staining the leaf tissue
options.feedback: Vivid red colouring regularly appears well before the first frost of the season, so frost damage isn't what's producing it.

items.ok_title: A pigment made fresh, not unmasked
items.ok_line: Unlike yellow, this colour is manufactured by the leaf specifically in autumn.
items.ko_title: Not more yellow, not decay, not frost
items.ko_line: This colour behaves differently from yellow because it's being actively produced, not revealed by the loss of something else.
items.exp_title: A colour built new, not uncovered
items.exp_text: Unlike the yellow and orange pigments that sit hidden in a leaf all summer, the red and purple pigments seen in autumn are manufactured fresh by the leaf's own cells specifically during that season, using sugar trapped inside the leaf as growth slows. Some trees, or some individual leaves catching more sunlight, produce far more of it than others of the same species, which is why the effect varies so much even on one tree. Researchers generally think this fresh pigment shields the leaf's tissue while it finishes salvaging its nutrients, acting something like a sunscreen for the final days of a leaf that is already on its way to falling.

items.prompt: What actually snaps a leaf free from its twig when it falls in autumn?

options.label: Wind alone tears the leaf away from a twig that would otherwise hold it firmly all winter
options.feedback: A leaf that has finished changing colour will drop on a calm, windless day just as readily as a windy one, so wind alone isn't what's cutting the connection.

options.label: The whole leaf stalk simply rots away from disease
options.feedback: This isn't disease or decay; the leaf separates cleanly and predictably at the same precise spot every single year on a perfectly healthy tree.

options.label: A special layer of weak-walled cells forms at the base of the leaf stalk and lets go once it's complete
options.feedback: That specialised layer, built at the base of every leaf stalk, weakens the connection there on cue, so the leaf eventually parts from the twig with barely any force needed.

options.label: The leaf simply becomes too heavy for the stalk to keep holding
options.feedback: A leaf's weight barely changes as autumn approaches, and a stalk that easily supported that same leaf all summer wouldn't suddenly fail under an unchanged load.

items.ok_title: A seam built to give way
items.ok_line: A weak layer of cells at the leaf's base is what finally lets go.
items.ko_title: Not wind, not rot, not weight
items.ko_line: The leaf separates at the exact same spot every year, which points to a structure built into that spot rather than an outside force.
items.exp_text: At the base of every leaf stalk, where it joins the twig, the tree builds a layer of cells with unusually weak walls, called an abscission layer. As autumn progresses those cells weaken further and the connective tissue running through that layer is gradually dismantled, until barely anything is left holding the leaf on. At that point even a light breeze, or sometimes no force at all, is enough to snap the leaf free at that prepared seam.

items.prompt: Why is a tree's autumn leaf-drop generally triggered by shortening day length rather than by dropping temperature?

options.label: Day length is a reliable seasonal calendar that never fluctuates unpredictably from year to year, unlike temperature, which can rise or fall out of season
options.feedback: Because the length of daylight on a given date changes on an utterly fixed and predictable schedule every year, using it as the trigger means the leaf-drop process starts right on time even during an unusually warm or unusually cold autumn.

options.label: Day length is easier for the leaf to physically measure than temperature
options.feedback: There's no comparison here of how easy each signal is to measure; the reason day length is used is that it stays reliably tied to the calendar, unlike temperature.

options.label: Shortening days directly cause the leaf stalk to grow longer and weaker
options.feedback: Shortening day length doesn't act on the stalk's length at all; it's detected as a signal that sets off the separate process of building the weak layer at the stalk's base.

options.label: Only day length changes at all during autumn; temperature stays essentially constant
options.feedback: Temperature clearly does drop through autumn in most places; the point isn't that temperature stays constant, but that it isn't a reliable enough calendar to trigger the process on schedule.

items.ok_line: Day length ticks by on a fixed schedule no warm or cold spell can throw off.
items.ko_title: Not ease of sensing, not stalk growth, not constant temperature
items.ko_line: The advantage of day length as a signal is specifically about how reliably it tracks the calendar, compared with a signal that can swing unpredictably.
items.exp_title: A signal the weather can't disturb
items.exp_text: A leaf contains a pigment sensitive to the balance of light and darkness across a day, letting the tree detect how the length of daylight is changing as the season turns. Because that balance shifts on an absolutely fixed schedule tied to the calendar, a tree using it as its cue for shedding leaves gets a trigger that never runs early or late due to a random hot or cold spell. Temperature, by contrast, can swing wildly within a single week, which would make it a far less dependable signal for timing something as important as when to let go of a whole season's worth of leaves.

items.prompt: Why is it worth a tree's effort to drop all its broad leaves before winter rather than simply keeping them through the cold months?

options.label: A broad leaf turns poisonous to the tree once winter arrives
options.feedback: Nothing about winter conditions turns the leaf's own tissue toxic to the tree that grew it; the actual problem is a practical one involving water, not any kind of poisoning.

options.label: Keeping leaves through winter would attract too many insects
options.feedback: Most insects are far less active in cold weather, so insect attraction isn't the pressure driving a tree to drop its broad leaves before winter.

options.label: Broad leaves would block too much sunlight from reaching the ground below
options.feedback: How much light reaches the ground beneath a tree isn't a problem the tree itself needs to solve, and it isn't the reason broad-leaved trees shed their leaves before winter.

options.label: A broad leaf would keep losing water through its thin surface all winter, at a time when frozen ground leaves the roots unable to replace it
options.feedback: Even a leaf sitting motionless in the cold still loses some water through its surface, and frozen soil can leave roots with nothing to draw on to replace that loss for months at a time.

items.ok_title: A leak the tree can no longer afford
items.ok_line: A leaf keeps leaking water even in winter, right when the roots can't refill it.
items.ko_title: Not poison, not insects, not shading the ground
items.ko_line: The pressure here comes down to a resource the tree can't replace during a frozen winter — think about what a thin, broad leaf constantly loses.
items.exp_text: Even in cold weather a thin broad leaf keeps losing some water vapour through its surface, a loss the roots normally replace easily by drawing on liquid water in the soil. Once the ground freezes solid, that soil water becomes unavailable to the roots even though it's technically still there, so any leaf still hanging on the tree keeps draining a supply that can no longer be topped up. Shedding every broad leaf before that freeze sets in removes the leak entirely, letting the tree simply wait out the winter without slowly drying itself out.

items.prompt: Why does the twig left behind after a leaf falls usually show a small, neat, closed scar rather than an open wound?

options.label: The falling leaf carries away a flap of twig skin that seals the wound as it tears off
options.feedback: The leaf comes away cleanly at the abscission layer without pulling any of the twig's own tissue along with it; nothing from the twig itself detaches with the leaf to cover the spot.

options.label: Sap immediately floods the site and hardens into a plug
options.feedback: This process is finished before the leaf ever separates, and it isn't a matter of sap rushing out to a fresh wound and hardening afterward.

options.label: The tree builds a corky protective layer across the base of the stalk before the leaf ever separates, sealing the spot from the inside first
options.feedback: By the time the leaf finally lets go, that protective layer is already in place, so what's left behind is a scar that was closed before the opening ever existed rather than an injury waiting to heal.

options.label: Insects and fungi quickly cover the spot with a protective coating
options.feedback: The neat, sealed scar shows up reliably on trees with no insect or fungal activity anywhere near it; the sealing is something the tree itself builds, not something added afterward by other organisms.

items.ok_line: The protective layer is built first; the leaf only lets go afterward.
items.ko_title: Not a torn flap, not sap, not outside help
items.ko_line: Think about the order of events here — is the twig sealed before the leaf separates, or does it scramble to heal an open wound afterward?
items.exp_text: As the abscission layer at the base of a leaf stalk develops, the tree also builds a corky, waterproof layer of cells directly beneath it, sealing off the twig's inner tissue from what will soon be exposed air. That protective layer is finished and in place before the connective tissue holding the leaf finally gives way. Because the sealing happens first, the moment the leaf actually detaches there is no raw wound left behind at all, only a scar that was already closed.

items.prompt: Why might a tree drop leaves from part of its crown in the middle of summer, well before any of the usual autumn colour change?

options.label: Severe drought stress can trigger the same leaf-dropping process that normally runs in autumn, cutting the tree's water losses early
options.feedback: The identical shedding machinery that normally responds to shortening autumn daylight can also be switched on by drought stress at any time of year, letting a struggling tree cut its water losses by sacrificing some leaves early.

options.label: This can only ever mean the tree is already dead
options.feedback: A tree dropping leaves under drought stress in summer is very often still alive and actively protecting itself, deliberately sacrificing some leaves rather than being a sign the whole tree has already died.

options.label: Direct sun damage burns through the leaf stalk
options.feedback: Sunlight doesn't physically burn through a leaf stalk; the shedding seen here comes from the tree's own internal signalling being triggered early, not from external heat damage to the stalk itself.

options.label: It happens completely at random and has no identifiable trigger
options.feedback: This kind of early leaf drop reliably tracks with drought stress rather than occurring at random, which points to it being triggered by a specific, identifiable condition.

items.ok_title: The same machinery, an earlier trigger
items.ok_line: Drought stress can flip the same switch that autumn normally flips.
items.ko_title: Not death, not sun damage, not random
items.ko_line: The same leaf-dropping process that runs every autumn can also be switched on by a different kind of stress, at any time of year.
items.exp_title: One mechanism, more than one trigger
items.exp_text: The abscission layer that severs a leaf stalk isn't wired only to the shortening daylight of autumn; it can also be activated by severe water shortage, since a leaf still open and losing water during a drought is a liability the tree can no longer afford. Dropping some leaves early reduces the total surface still leaking water, helping the rest of the tree conserve what moisture it has left. The tree is using the very same shedding process it would normally save for autumn, just switched on by a different kind of stress instead of the usual seasonal signal.

items.prompt: Why do conifers still look green all through winter even though they do shed some of their needles too?

options.label: Conifer needles are chemically incapable of ever separating from the tree
options.feedback: Conifer needles clearly do separate and fall, which is why they collect on the ground beneath the tree; the difference from broadleaf trees is in the pace and pattern of that shedding, not in whether it can happen at all.

options.label: Conifers replace every needle overnight, so the crown is never without a full set
options.feedback: There's no single overnight replacement event here; needle turnover happens gradually across several years rather than as a single rapid swap.

options.label: Conifer needles contain a pigment that stays green even after the needle has died and dropped
options.feedback: A needle that has separated from the tree and fallen isn't what keeps the crown looking green; the canopy's appearance depends on which needles are still attached to the tree at any given time.

options.label: Conifers only drop a portion of their oldest needles at a time, a few years apart, so the canopy is never left bare
options.feedback: With only the oldest needles shed in any given stretch, and a fresh younger set staying attached throughout, the crown as a whole always keeps enough needles in place to look continuously green.

items.ok_title: Shed a few at a time, never all at once
items.ok_line: Only the oldest needles go, spread out over years, so the crown never empties.
items.ko_title: Not incapable, not overnight, not a lingering colour
items.ko_line: Conifers do lose needles; the question is about the pace and pattern of that loss compared with a broadleaf tree's.
items.exp_text: A broadleaf tree typically drops nearly its entire crown of leaves within days once its autumn shedding process begins, leaving the whole tree bare at once. A conifer instead sheds only its oldest needles, generally those several years old, a modest portion at a time, while younger needles from more recent years remain firmly attached and functioning. Because at any moment most of the crown is made up of needles that are nowhere near ready to be shed, the tree keeps a continuously green appearance right through the very same winter that leaves a broadleaf tree standing completely bare.

items.prompt: Once the abscission layer starts forming at the base of a leaf stalk, what happens to the leaf's own supply of water and sugar before it ever detaches?

options.label: Nothing changes until the moment of separation, when both are cut off instantly
options.feedback: The blockage inside the abscission layer builds up gradually as the layer develops, rather than staying fully open right up until the instant the leaf finally detaches.

options.label: The layer gradually blocks the transport tubes running through it, so the leaf becomes cut off from fresh water and sugar days before it actually falls
options.feedback: As the abscission layer develops, the transport tubes running through that narrow strip of tissue become increasingly obstructed, choking off the leaf's connection to the rest of the tree well before the stalk finally gives way.

options.label: Extra water and sugar are pumped into the leaf right before it falls, to nourish the ground below
options.feedback: The direction of any late-stage transport across the abscission layer runs toward salvaging material for the tree, not toward sending extra resources out to the leaf to be dropped onto the ground.

options.label: The leaf begins drawing water and sugar from neighbouring leaves instead of from the twig
options.feedback: There's no route for one leaf to start drawing supplies from a completely separate leaf; whatever the leaf receives has to travel through the very connection at its own stalk that is being blocked.

items.ok_title: Cut off well before the fall
items.ok_line: The transport tubes get blocked days ahead of the leaf actually letting go.
items.ko_title: Not instant, not extra supply, not borrowed from neighbours
items.ko_line: The blockage builds up gradually as the layer forms, and it runs in one direction — think about which side loses its supply.
items.exp_title: Cut off before it ever falls
items.exp_text: As the abscission layer develops at the base of the stalk, the narrow transport tubes for water and sugar running through that same strip of tissue become increasingly blocked by the very cell changes building the layer. Days before the leaf finally separates, it is effectively running on whatever water and sugar it already had stored, with almost nothing fresh still arriving from the twig. That isolation, arriving well ahead of the actual fall, helps explain why a leaf's colour and condition can decline sharply in its final days even while it's still firmly attached.
